1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. LLM: large language model; API: application programming interface; JSON: JavaScript Object Notation; SDK: software development kit; CI/CD: continuous integration and continuous delivery; PR: pull request

  • Turning business requirements into functional, non-functional and infrastructure requirements for a Claude application
  • The systems life cycle for an LLM application, including evals, versioning and retirement
  • Software engineering foundations: REST APIs and JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, SDLC integration, code review, refactoring

2Understanding Requirements

Running case

Tidewater Insurance Wants a Claims Assistant

  • Business goal: "Cut the time adjusters spend reading claim files"
  • Constraints: files hold personal data, adjusters wait for answers, and the budget is limited
  • Your job: turn that sentence into requirements a team can build and test

Requirements start from the business requirement and the solution architecture. Split them into three kinds:

Kind Question it answers Claims assistant example
Functional What must the system do? Summarize a claim file, answer questions about a policy, cite the source page
Non-functional How well, how fast, how safely, at what cost? First answer in under 5 seconds, cost per claim under a limit, answers grounded in the file, PII protected
Infrastructure Where and on what does it run? Which API platform (first-party or a cloud provider), region and data residency, rate limits and capacity, secrets storage, logging

  • Every requirement needs a measurable acceptance criterion (a number or a pass/fail check). Those criteria become your evals (Module 16).
  • The classic LLM trade-off is quality, latency and cost: you rarely maximize all three, so rank them from the requirement. Waiting users drive latency; overnight work drives cost.
  • Requirements also decide the API choice (real-time or batch), the model tier and whether tools or retrieval are needed.
Exam tip

In a requirement-driven question, underline the binding constraint (latency, cost, compliance, data residency) and choose the option that satisfies that constraint first.

Exam tip

A requirement without a measurable acceptance criterion cannot become an eval, so it is not yet a requirement.

3Systems Life Cycle

Phase What changes for an LLM application
Requirements and design Pick API, model, tools; write acceptance criteria
Build Prompts, tools, schemas and configuration live in version control
Test Evals with graded examples run on every change; unit tests for tool code
Deploy Pin the model version; roll out gradually; feature-flag prompt changes
Operate Monitor quality, latency, cost, error rates; log request IDs and traces
Maintain Update prompts, dependencies and models; re-run evals; handle model retirement
Retire Migrate before the model's retirement date; archive data
  • Prompts are code: version them, review them, test them, and roll them back.
  • A model change is a release: re-run the evals before and after, because behavior can change between model versions (Module 8).

4Software Engineering Foundations

REST APIs and JSON

  • The Claude API is a REST API over HTTPS with JSON request and response bodies. You send a POST with headers (API key, version) and a JSON body; the client SDKs wrap this.
  • Know the status code classes: 4xx means the request is wrong or not allowed (do not retry unchanged), 5xx or an overloaded response means a transient server condition (retry with backoff), 429 means a rate limit (honor retry-after).
  • Idempotency: a retry must not repeat a side effect. A model call is safe to repeat; a tool that charges a card is not, so give tool actions an idempotency key.

Asynchronous programming

  • Calls to Claude are slow (seconds), so use async I/O (async/await, an async client) to run many requests concurrently instead of one after another.
  • Bound the concurrency with a semaphore or a worker pool: too many parallel calls cause 429 errors (Module 3). Add exponential backoff with jitter for retries.
  • Streaming (server-sent events) shows text as it arrives and helps perceived latency; the code consumes events as an async stream.

Version control, SDLC integration, code review, refactoring

Practice For Claude applications
Version control Commit prompts, schemas, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md; never commit API keys; use branches and pull requests
SDLC integration Run evals and tests in CI/CD; use Claude Code in pipelines (-p) for review and test generation
Code review Review prompt and tool changes like code; use an independent Claude instance, not the one that wrote the change, for AI-assisted review
Small refactors Direct edits with tests running; one change at a time
Large refactors Plan first (explore, then plan), write or keep tests, change in small verified steps, review diffs; use plan mode in Claude Code
Exam tip

A refactor touching many files is made safe by tests first and small, verified steps, with a plan before edits.

5Exam Q&A

S1Tidewater's business goal is "faster answers for adjusters". Which statement is a measurable non-functional requirement?

  • AThe first token of an answer must appear within five seconds for 95 percent of requests
  • BThe assistant has a nice interface
  • CThe assistant should be helpful, friendly and pleasant to every person who uses it
  • DThe assistant uses Claude
Show the answer

Answer: A. A non-functional requirement states a measurable quality such as latency with a threshold; the others are vague or are design choices.

S2A requirement says claim files must be processed only in a specific geographic region. Which kind of requirement is this, and what does it influence?

  • AFunctional; it changes the prompt
  • BNone; the API decides the region
  • CNon-functional only; it has no technical effect on the system
  • DInfrastructure; it influences the platform and region choice
Show the answer

Answer: D. Data residency is an infrastructure requirement that constrains where requests run.

S3A team ranks its constraints: cost first, answers needed by the next morning, quality must be good. What does this point to?

  • AAsynchronous (batch) processing with a model sized to the quality bar
  • BStreaming with a high output limit
  • CParallel synchronous calls without limits
  • DA real-time API with the largest model for every single claim, to be safe
Show the answer

Answer: A. Cost-first, latency-tolerant work fits batch processing; model size follows the quality bar proven by evals.

S4Which life-cycle practice makes a prompt change safe to release?

  • AAsk a colleague whether the new wording looks fine to them
  • BVersion the prompt, run the evals, and keep a rollback
  • CWait for users to report problems
  • DEdit the prompt directly in production, then watch the feedback
Show the answer

Answer: B. Prompts are code: version them and test them with evals before and after the change.

S5A provider announces that the model your application uses will retire in six months. What should the team do?

  • ARemove the model setting so the platform picks one automatically for us
  • BIgnore it until the day of retirement
  • CPlan a migration: test a newer model with the evals, adjust prompts, and release before the retirement date
  • DSwitch to the oldest available model, since it will never be retired
Show the answer

Answer: C. A model change is a release; test it with evals and migrate before the date.

S6An application sends 500 independent requests one after another and takes too long. What is the most effective improvement?

  • AUse async I/O with bounded concurrency and backoff on rate limits
  • BUse a longer timeout
  • CRun all 500 requests at once without any limit on concurrency, retries or backoff
  • DRemove the system prompt
Show the answer

Answer: A. Concurrency overlaps the waiting time; bounding it and backing off avoids rate-limit errors.

S7A tool that issues a refund fails with a network timeout, and the application retries it. What protects the customer?

  • AA larger max_tokens
  • BNothing; retries are always safe because the model call is repeatable
  • CAn idempotency key so a repeat does not issue a second refund
  • DRetrying faster
Show the answer

Answer: C. Idempotency prevents a repeated side effect when a call is retried.

S8A developer commits ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in a configuration file. What is the right action?

  • AEncode it in base64
  • BRotate the key, remove it from history, and load it from a secrets manager
  • CShorten the key
  • DLeave it as it is, because the repository is private and only the team can read the file
Show the answer

Answer: B. A committed secret is compromised: rotate it and keep keys out of version control.

S9A change touches 60 files across a service. Which approach is safest with Claude Code?

  • AEdit all files in parallel without tests
  • BExplore and plan first, keep tests passing, and apply the change in small verified steps with review
  • CAsk for the whole change in one big step, then merge it without review or tests
  • DRewrite the service from scratch
Show the answer

Answer: B. Large refactors need a plan, tests and small steps.

S10Which TWO belong in a requirements list for the claims assistant? Select TWO.

  • AA promise that the model never makes mistakes
  • BA functional requirement: summarize a claim file and cite the source page
  • CAn infrastructure requirement: records must stay in one region and keys in a secrets manager
  • DA mood for the logo
  • EThe font of the user interface
Show the answer

Answer: B, C. Functional and infrastructure requirements are concrete and testable; the other items are cosmetic or unachievable.

S11Which TWO practices keep AI-assisted code review reliable? Select TWO.

  • ARunning tests and evals in CI alongside the review
  • BSkipping review when the diff is small
  • CAsking the generating session to approve its own change
  • DDisabling the tests to speed things up
  • EReviewing with an independent instance that did not write the change
Show the answer

Answer: A, E. An independent reviewer and automated tests catch what self-review misses.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Requirements Functional (what), non-functional (how well: latency, cost, quality, security), infrastructure (where: platform, region, limits, secrets)
Acceptance criteria Measurable; they become evals
Trade-off Quality, latency, cost; the binding constraint decides
Life cycle Requirements → design → build → test (evals) → deploy → operate → maintain → retire
Prompts Code: version, review, test, roll back; pin model versions
REST/JSON 4xx do not retry unchanged; 5xx or overload retry with backoff; 429 honor retry-after; idempotency for side effects
Async Bounded concurrency, backoff with jitter, streaming for perceived latency
Version control Commit prompts and config, never keys; PRs
Refactoring Plan, tests first, small verified steps; independent review
